content:
At school I had three maths classes a week, forty weeks a year, and we covered maybe three theorems per class. That is about 360 theorems a year, 3,600 in ten years of school. I always wondered how that compares with the proof of Fermat's Last Theorem.

With a Lean formalisation available it can finally be counted: about 30,000 declarations sit under fermat_last_theorem (some 21,000 of them theorems), and the longest chain of dependencies is 117 steps deep. At my school's pace that is sixty to eighty more years of classes. (A Lean lemma is smaller than a textbook theorem, and everything borrowed from Mathlib is not counted at all, so take this as a sense of scale, not a measurement.)

So I built a map of it, and of two other large formalisations: https://landofproof.com

I love that people are playing with the FLT proof like this!

I guess I also love that FLT is clearly much deeper than Navier-Stokes because the graph is much bigger ;-)

Luigi Massacci said:

or the proof is much worse ; - )

The FLT proof formalized was one which was written by human experts a year or so after Wiles' proof, so people had had the time to digest and simplify some of the arguments. The NS proof has not yet been digested at all. So this is not an unreasonable hypothesis (although I don't think Wiles' proof was made 20x easier, and of course most of the FLT proof was not due to Wiles in some sense and had already been digested to a large extent).

There is probably something to be said that the NS proof is a counter-example, whereas FLT is an actual proof. When the unforced version of NS gets resolved, it might get resolved in the positive, and we'll see how long the proof is. It might be longer than FLT.

Utensil Song said:

How to intuitively understand why there are the big clusters of nodes that feels like largely interconnected?

It's the dominator-tree view of the Navier–Stokes proof.

https://landofproof.com/?source=ns&h=dm&x=690104&y=471391&z=0.05912&mode=path&depth=1

Lemma X dominates Y if every chain of dependencies from the main theorem down to Y passes through X. Each circle is one gateway lemma's territory: everything the main theorem can only reach through it, minus sub-territories big enough to get their own circle. The big blob is a territory that never splits further: one lemma has about 9,000 theorems directly under it, and they cite each other heavily. In circles that large the dots are packed on a spiral, so position inside a circle means little; about three quarters of Navier–Stokes theorems sit in such circles. Splitting them further is on the to-do list - haven't figured out how to visualize it in a better way
Are there many gigantic proofs like N-S and FLT in modern mathematics

The proof of FLT is tiny compared to some of what has happened since in Langlands, which builds upon the ideas of Wiles and many others. I don't know why you call the proof of N-S gigantic, look at the size of the lean proofs yourself. The FLT code is 30x as large and only represents what number theorists could do in 1995, which is a long time ago. Langlandsy number theory builds on its earlier successes, that is the nature of the field. N-S is tiny in comparison.
Is it realistic to expect that Langlands program (what is currently known) to be formalized. Maybe it is possible with the current AI

Nobody has a clue how to prove Langlands' conjectures for general number fields (recent breakthroughs only work for certain types of number fields and 0% of number fields have this property). This is in stark contrast to N-S where humans were well on the way to proving it and AI just did the last mile. I don't think it's unfeasible that the global Langlands conjectures for number fields will still be open in ten years' time. It's not clear to me how many big new ideas will be needed to resolve them. Maybe 0 (in which case AI will do it), maybe 10 (in which case maybe they'll resist).

As for formalizing what is known, this could be done in a slop way with sufficient money, but that is true for an arbitrary correctly-proved mathematical statement.

Anh Nguyễn said:

Are there many gigantic proofs like N-S and FLT in modern mathematics

Wikipedia has a short list of long mathematical proofs, but it is far from comprehensive. You probably want to draw a distinction between proofs that seem to unavoidably involve big computer calculations, and those that do not. FLT is in the former category, as is the classification of finite simple groups. But if your measure is simply the length of a Lean proof (which doesn't "cheat" using things like native_decide), then things like the proof of the Kepler conjecture or the 5th Schur number will win hands down.

I launched a Prove2Me campaign to (fully) formalize Mazur Torsion Theorem. In case anyone wants to tell their agents to work on it, here is the campaign: https://prove2.me/missions/Mazur%E2%80%99s_Torsion_Theorem%3A_Full_Classification_and_All_Fifteen_Groups/milestones
Seems to be going fairly well so far.
Thank you for the Wiki links. I want to know more about “deep” proofs than long technical proofs
And I want to ask that how small/big is the FLT proofs compare to modern (2026) proofs
